misconception_description: Student believes that the arithmetic operation + has higher precedence than the arithmetic operation /.

solutions.generated_code:
program DamagePokemon
kamus
  attackerTipe, defenderTipe : string
  attackerLevel, defenderLevel : integer
  efektivitas : real
  selisihLevel, damage : integer
algoritma
  input(attackerTipe, attackerLevel)
  input(defenderTipe, defenderLevel)
  if attackerTipe == "fire" and defenderTipe == "grass" then
    efektivitas <- 2
  else if attackerTipe == "grass" and defenderTipe == "water" then
    efektivitas <- 2
  else if attackerTipe == "water" and defenderTipe == "fire" then
    efektivitas <- 2
  else if attackerTipe == "grass" and defenderTipe == "fire" then
    efektivitas <- 0.5
  else if attackerTipe == "water" and defenderTipe == "grass" then
    efektivitas <- 0.5
  else if attackerTipe == "fire" and defenderTipe == "water" then
    efektivitas <- 0.5
  else
    efektivitas <- 1
  endif
  selisihLevel <- attackerLevel - defenderLevel
  damage <- bulat((((2 * attackerLevel) / 5) + 2) * (attackerLevel / defenderLevel) * efektivitas * selisihLevel / 10)
  if damage < 1 then
    damage <- 1
  endif
  output(damage)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student has added explicit parentheses around all division operations in the damage calculation formula: `(((2 * attacker_level) / 5) + 2)` instead of `((2 * attacker_level) / 5 + 2)`, `((attacker_level / defender_level))` with extra parentheses, and `(level_diff / 10)` instead of `level_diff / 10`. The student believes that addition has higher precedence than division, so they think they need to explicitly parenthesize division operations to ensure they are evaluated before any additions. Without these parentheses, they believe the additions would be evaluated first. In reality, division already has higher precedence than addition, so these extra parentheses are unnecessary but don't change the result. The code still produces correct output, but the unnecessary defensive parenthesization reveals the student's misconception about operator precedence.
